notes.meaning: Judah received the first allotment of land in Canaan by sacred lot. This vast southern region reached from the border of Edom to the dry Wilderness of Zin. Judah was given the lead position among the tribes because God had promised royal leadership to this tribe.

Judah's southern border began at the south end of the Salt Sea (the Dead Sea) and ran westward across the desert to the Mediterranean Sea. The line passed through the scorpion-infested Ascent of Akrabbim, went south of Kadesh-barnea, and followed the Brook of Egypt. This line marked not only Judah's territory, but also the southern boundary of the entire Promised Land.

On the east, Judah's boundary was the entire length of the Salt Sea, ending where the Jordan River flows into it. The northern border started right at that same spot, at the northern bay where the river meets the sea. This formed a clear and natural water boundary along the eastern side of Judah's land.

The northern line climbed from the Jordan valley past Beth-hoglah and ran north of Beth-arabah toward the hill country. It also ran by the Stone of Bohan, a landmark named after a leader from the tribe of Reuben. This boundary separated the territory of Judah from the land later given to Benjamin.

The boundary continued upward from the Valley of Achor toward Debir and turned north toward Gilgal, near the steep pass of Adummim. It then followed the waters of En-shemesh and ended at the spring of En-rogel, just outside Jerusalem. The Valley of Achor served as a quiet reminder of the trouble caused earlier by Achan's sin.

The border climbed through the Valley of Hinnom, just south of the Jebusite city of Jerusalem, and went up to the ridge overlooking the Valley of Rephaim. This placed Jerusalem right on the border between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin. Later in Israel's history, the Valley of Hinnom became infamous for idol worship, while Jerusalem became the royal capital under King David.

From the ridge west of Jerusalem, the boundary line curved toward the spring of Nephtoah and the hills of Mount Ephron. It then turned toward Baalah, an important town also known as Kiriath-jearim. This town later became famous as the resting place of God's sacred chest, the ark of the covenant, for twenty years.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that an ancient Egyptian papyrus mentions the 'wells of Merneptah' in Canaan, suggesting the name Nephtoah may refer to Pharaoh Merneptah.

notes.meaning: From Kiriath-jearim, the border turned westward toward Mount Seir, passing along the ridge of Chesalon. It then dropped down to Beth-shemesh and crossed over to Timnah. Beth-shemesh was located on the edge of the foothills and later became famous when the Philistines returned the ark of the Lord there.

The boundary line continued along the northern slope of Ekron, curved past Shikkeron and Mount Baalah, and reached Jabneel. From there, it finally ended at the Mediterranean Sea. Ekron was a major Philistine city that fell inside Judah's assigned borders, though Philistines still lived in the region.

The western boundary of Judah was the Mediterranean coastline itself, known as the Great Sea. These outer borders completely encircled the land assigned to the clans of Judah. God gave the land to individual families and clans so that every household had a secure inheritance.

Just as the LORD had commanded Moses, Joshua gave Caleb his special share of land inside Judah's territory. This portion included Hebron, an ancient city originally founded by Arba, the father of the giant Anakim. Joshua was faithful to honor God's promise to his longtime friend and fellow spy.

Caleb drove out the three Anakim clan leaders—Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai—from the hill country of Hebron. These were the very giants that had terrified the other ten spies forty-five years earlier. Caleb's great victory was a direct reward for his wholehearted trust in God's power.

After taking Hebron, Caleb marched against the nearby fortified town of Debir, which was once called Kiriath-sepher. That older name means 'city of books,' suggesting it may have been a center where ancient records or writings were kept. Caleb was eager to secure the full territory God had promised him.

Caleb challenged the warriors in his army by promising his daughter Acsah in marriage to whoever could conquer Kiriath-sepher. Debir was a strong fortress, so Caleb offered a high reward to inspire courage in a younger generation of fighters. He showed boldness himself and wanted to raise up bold leaders around him.

Caleb's nephew Othniel answered the call, captured the fortress, and received Acsah as his wife. This brave deed kept the family land together and proved Othniel's courage. God was preparing Othniel here for a greater task, as he later became Israel's very first judge.

As Acsah was going to her new home, she urged Othniel to ask her father for a field. When she got down from her donkey to make the request herself, Caleb asked what she needed. She approached her father with humility and deep respect, and Caleb was ready to listen.

Acsah asked her father for a blessing, meaning an extra gift of land that had water. The land she had received in the Negev was dry and baked by the heat, so it needed a good water source to support life and crops. Caleb generously granted her request by giving her both the upper and lower springs.

A summary statement marks the close of the border description and introduces the list of Judah's towns. God had given the tribe of Judah a huge and fruitful inheritance for all their clans. The verses that follow list the actual cities that belonged to them within these borders.

The list begins with the southern towns of Judah in the dry region known as the Negev, bordering Edom. This was the first of four main regions into which Judah's cities were divided. Although some of these towns were remote desert outposts, God recorded every one as part of His people's promised home.
